lines.text: Academic life at a British university follows a structured rhythm of terms, assessments, and intellectual growth. The academic year typically runs from September to June, divided into three terms: autumn (Michaelmas at Oxford and Cambridge), spring (Hilary/Lent), and summer (Trinity/Easter). Students attend lectures, participate in seminars, complete coursework, and sit examinations. Assessment methods vary: essays test critical thinking and argument, exams test knowledge under pressure, presentations develop communication skills, and group projects build teamwork. Academic integrity is paramount — plagiarism (presenting others' work as your own) carries severe penalties, from mark reduction to expulsion. Referencing systems (Harvard, APA, MHRA) ensure proper attribution of sources. The supervisor relationship is central to postgraduate study — your supervisor guides your research, provides feedback, and helps shape your thesis or dissertation. Academic writing has its own conventions: formal register, hedging language ('It could be argued that...'), evidence-based claims, and structured argumentation. Office hours allow students to discuss work individually with lecturers. Academic progression moves through undergraduate (bachelor's degree), postgraduate taught (master's degree), and postgraduate research (PhD/doctorate). External examiners from other universities ensure standards remain consistent. The viva voce — an oral examination defending your PhD thesis — is the final hurdle of doctoral study, a tradition that has defined academic life for centuries.

lines.text: British academic titles differ from American ones. 'Professor' in the UK is the highest academic rank — not all lecturers are professors. 'Dr' indicates a doctorate. Addressing academics correctly (Professor Smith, Dr Khan, or by first name if invited) shows respect and awareness.
lines.name: British academic titles differ from American ones. 'Professor' in the UK is the highest academic rank — not all lecturers are professors. 'Dr' indicates a doctorate. Addressing academics correctly (Professor Smith, Dr Khan, or by first name if invited) shows respect and awareness.

lines.text: 'Office hours' — set times when lecturers are available for student consultations — are standard. Saying 'I'll come to your office hours' is the natural phrase. Emailing first to check availability is common courtesy, especially for busy academics.

lines.text: Turnitin is plagiarism-detection software used by virtually all UK universities. Students submit work through it, and it generates a 'similarity report' showing any matching text. 'Running it through Turnitin' has become standard academic vocabulary.
